## Memory, Prediction & Energy Costs

Neural systems must learn and predict under limits on memory, activity, and energy. I use information theory and computational models to investigate how these constraints shape biological adaptation and how they can inform artificial and hybrid neural architectures.

Since 2026, I have been a postdoctoral researcher at [Scripps College](https://www.scrippscollege.edu/), working with [Professor Sarah Marzen](https://www.sarahmarzen.com/) on memory, prediction, and energy efficiency in neural systems. This work contributes to the [Hybrid-AI collaboration](https://hybrid-ai.umd.edu/), which includes the University of Maryland and investigates hybrid artificial–living neural networks for learning and prediction.

## Current Academic Research

The project examines predictive information in continuous-time stochastic processes, memory and adaptation in spiking neural networks, and the energetic costs of neural computation. Biological mechanisms provide a starting point for asking how computational resources can be used more efficiently.

**[Hybrid Adaptive Networks](../../projects/hybrid-adaptive-networks.qmd)** is ongoing research with Sarah Marzen's group. The first manuscript is in preparation.

## Related Independent AI Research

With Raymond Aschheim, I co-authored **The Lock-In Phase Hypothesis: Identity Consolidation as a Precursor to AGI** [@amaral2025lockin]. This 2025 preprint proposes a transition toward more stable goals and behavior in language models, develops measures of consolidation, and reports model-dependent experiments. Its proposed connection to AGI remains a hypothesis. This work is separate from my Scripps postdoctoral project.

For corporate research and consulting in AI and quantum computing, see [Gauge Freedom](../../venture/index.qmd).
